findings.page: PDF p. 60 (printed p. 36); taxonomy at PDF p. 19–20 (printed p. xv–xvi)
findings.chapter: Ch. 2 — What Actually Happens During Inference (§2.5 Common Mistakes)
findings.evidence: §2.5 (PDF p. 60): "actual sustained bandwidth for weight-read kernels may be 60–80% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE: industry rule of thumb, no named survey or benchmark][HYPOTHESIS][UNMEASURED] — not measured or cited here." The Preface (PDF p. 19) defines the Axis-1 provenance values as "[1P] — first-party: the model vendor's own spec. / [canonical scenario] — the book's own internally defined workload and model / [ILLUSTRATIVE] — a non-canonical worked-example or scenario input chosen to make a calculation concrete / [2°] — reputable second-hand / [LAB] — measured on the author's own home-lab hardware", and (PDF p. 20) states: "A label pair always takes one item from each of the first two axes, e.g. [1P][DERIVED] or [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]; the two tags are set with no space between them and never break across a line."
findings.issue: The tag '[ILLUSTRATIVE: industry rule of thumb, no named survey or benchmark]' is not one of the defined Axis-1 provenance values — it embeds a free-text qualifier inside the tag, then adds a second and third axis token, producing a three-part label with an undefined first element. Everywhere else the book uses the closed vocabulary (e.g. '[ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS]', '[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION][DERIVED]'), so a reader or parser following the Preface's taxonomy cannot resolve this label to a defined provenance value. The substance (an unmeasured industry rule of thumb flagged as a hypothesis) is legitimate; only the tag form is malformed.
findings.fix_instruction: Normalize the label to the defined vocabulary: write '[ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS][UNMEASURED]' and move the qualifier out of the tag into the surrounding prose (e.g. 'may be 60–80% of peak — an industry rule of thumb, with no named survey or benchmark [ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS][UNMEASURED]'), matching the pattern already used elsewhere in the same chapter and in Ch. 4 §4.5.

findings.evidence: Page 29, Table 2-2, row 'Prefill: single-H100 capacity': '1.29 PFLOP / ~1.08 s ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS demand > 0.989 PFLOPS H100 peak; with the attention term included (~1.51 PFLOP) the demand is ~1.40 PFLOPS...'
findings.issue:
Arithmetic Error in Derived Value. The text states that including the attention term results in a demand of '~1.40 PFLOPS'. However, using the stated total FLOPs (~1.51 PFLOP) and the stated time (~1.08 s), the calculation is 1.51 / 1.08 ≈ 1.398, which rounds to ~1.40. Wait, re-reading the previous section (page 31, Table 2-2 scope note) and the text on page 29: 'with the attention term included (~1.51 PFLOP) the demand is ~1.40 PFLOPS'. Let's check the linear-only demand: 1.29 / 1.08 = 1.194 -> 1.19. The text claims 1.51 PFLOPs results in 1.40 PFLOPS. 1.51 / 1.08 = 1.398. This is technically correct rounding. However, earlier in §2.3.1 (Table 2-2), the row says 'Prefill: FLOPs, linear term only... 1.29 PFLOP... excludes... attention term, which adds ~0.22 PFLOP (+17%)... -> ~1.51 PFLOP total'. 1.29 + 0.22 = 1.51. 1.51/1.08 = 1.398. The text says 1.40. This is correct. 

Let's look at another spot. Page 56, Figure 2.2 caption: 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte'. Ridge = Peak FLOPS / Peak Bandwidth. 989 TFLOPS = 989 * 10^12 FLOP/s. 3.35 TB/s = 3.35 * 10^12 Byte/s. 989 / 3.35 ≈ 295.22. This is correct.
findings.fix_instruction: No defect found in this specific check. The arithmetic in Table 2-2 and Fig 2.2 is consistent.
